Okay, so I'm trying to figure out which substance, when mixed with water, produces the best conductor of electricity. The options given are table salt (A), granulated sugar (B), carbon dioxide (C), and motor oil (D). 

First, I remember from basic chemistry that table salt, which is sodium chloride (NaCl), is a strong electrolyte. That means when you dissolve it in water, it breaks down into sodium (Na+) and chloride (Cl−) ions. These ions are charged and can move freely in the water, allowing the solution to conduct electricity well.

On the other hand, granulated sugar, which is sucrose, is a non-electrolyte. Unlike table salt, sucrose doesn't dissolve into ions in water. Instead, it stays as molecules, which don't carry a charge. This means sugar water doesn't conduct electricity very well because there are no free ions to carry the current.

Carbon dioxide, when dissolved in water, forms a weak acid called carbonic acid. This doesn't release many ions, so the conductivity is very low. Lastly, motor oil is nonpolar and doesn't mix well with water. Since oil and water don't interact, there's no significant ion formation, so motor oil doesn't contribute to conductivity either.

I think the confusion might come from thinking that sugar might conduct electricity a bit because it's a solute, but in reality, it doesn't because it doesn't ionize. Maybe some people might confuse it with electrolytes, but that's not the case.

I also recall that in experiments, salt solutions conduct electricity much better than sugar solutions. So, table salt should be the best conductor among the options given.
</think>
